CHAPTER LXXX

THE CLOISTER

Brother Clement had taught and preached in Basle more than a
twelvemonth, when one day Jerome stood before him, dusty, with a
triumphant glance in his eye.

“Give the glory to God, Brother Clement; thou canst now wend to England
with me.”

“I am ready, Brother Jerome; and expecting thee these many months, have
in the intervals of teaching and devotion studied the English tongue
somewhat closely.”

“'Twas well thought of,” said Jerome. He then told him he had but
delayed till he could obtain extraordinary powers from the Pope to
collect money for the Church's use in England, and to hear confession
in all the secular monasteries. “So now gird up thy loins, and let us go
forth and deal a good blow for the Church, and against the Franciscans.”

The two friars went preaching down the Rhine for England. In the larger
places they both preached. At the smaller they often divided, and took
different sides of the river, and met again at some appointed spot. Both
were able orators, but in different styles.

Jerome's was noble and impressive, but a little contracted in religious
topics, and a trifle monotonous in delivery compared with Clement's,
though in truth not so, compared with most preachers.

Clement's was full of variety, and often remarkably colloquial. In its
general flow, tender and gently winning, it curled round the reason and
the heart. But it always rose with the rising thought; and so at times
Clement soared as far above Jerome as his level speaking was below him.
Indeed, in these noble heats he was all that we hue read of inspired
prophet or heathen orator: Vehemens ut procella, excitatus ut torrens,
incensus ut fulmen, tonabat, fulgurabat, et rapidis eloquentiae
fiuctibus cuncta proruebat et perturbabat.

I would give literal specimens, but for five objections; it is
difficult; time is short; I have done it elsewhere; an able imitator
has since done it better and similarity, a virtue in peas, is a vice in
books.

But (not to evade the matter entirely) Clement used secretly to try and
learn the recent events and the besetting sin of each town he was to
preach in.

But Jerome, the unbending, scorned to go out of his way for any people's
vices. At one great town, some leagues from the Rhine, they mounted
the same pulpit in turn. Jerome preached against vanity in dress, a
favourite theme of his. He was eloquent and satirical, and the people
listened with complacency. It was a vice that they were little given to.

Clement preached against drunkenness. It was a besetting sin, and sacred
from preaching in these parts: for the clergy themselves were infected
with it, and popular prejudice protected it, Clement dealt it merciless
blows out of Holy Writ and worldly experience. A crime itself, it was
the nursing mother of most crimes, especially theft and murder. He
reminded them of a parricide that had lately been committed in their
town by all honest man in liquor; and also how a band of drunkards had
roasted one of their own comrades alive at a neighbouring village. “Your
last prince,” said he, “is reported to have died of apoplexy, but well
you know he died of drink; and of your aldermen one perished miserably
last month dead drunk, suffocated in a puddle. Your children's backs go
bare that you may fill your bellies with that which makes you the
worst of beasts, silly as calves, yet fierce as boars; and drives your
families to need, and your souls to hell. I tell ye your town, ay, and
your very nation, would sink to the bottom of mankind did your women
drink as you do. And how long will they be temperate, and contrary to
nature, resist the example of their husbands and fathers? Vice ne'er
yet stood still. Ye must amend yourselves, or see them come down to
your mark, Already in Bohemia they drink along with the men. How shows
a drunken woman? Would you love to see your wives drunken, your mothers
drunken?” At this there was a shout of horror, for mediaeval audiences
had not learned to sit mumchance at a moving sermon. “Ah, that comes
home to you,” cried the friar. “What madmen! think you it doth not
more shock the all-pure God to see a man, His noblest work, turned to
a drunken beast, than it can shock you creatures of sin and unreason to
see a woman turned into a thing no better nor worse than yourselves.”

He ended with two pictures: a drunkard's house and family, and a sober
man's; both so true and dramatic in all their details that the wives
fell all to “ohing” and “ahing,” and “Eh, but that is a true word.”

This discourse caused quite all uproar. The hearers formed knots; the
men were indignant; so the women flattered them and took their part
openly against the preacher. A married man had a right to a drop; he
needed it, working for all the family. And for their part they did not
care to change their men for milksops.

The double faces! That very evening a hand of men caught near a hundred
of them round Brother Clement, filling his wallet with the best, and
offering him the very roses off their heads, and kissing his frock, and
blessing him “for taking in hand to mend their sots.”

Jerome thought this sermon too earthly.

“Drunkenness is not heresy, Clement, that a whole sermon should be
preached against it.”

As they went on, he found to his surprise that Clement's sermons sank
into his hearers deeper than his own; made them listen, think, cry, and
sometimes even amend their ways. “He hath the art of sinking to their
peg,” thought Jerome, “Yet he can soar high enough at times.”

Upon the whole it puzzled Jerome, who had a secret sense of superiority
to his tenderer brother. And after about two hundred miles of it, it
got to displease him as well as puzzle him. But he tried to check this
sentiment as petty and unworthy. “Souls differ like locks,” said he,
“and preachers must differ like keys, or the fewer should the Church
open for God to pass in. And certes, this novice hath the key to these
northern souls, being himself a northern man.”

And so they came slowly down the Rhine, sometimes drifting a few miles
down the stream; but in general walking by the banks preaching, and
teaching, and confessing sinners in the towns and villages; and they
reached the town of Dusseldorf.

There was the little quay where Gerard and Denys had taken boat up the
Rhine, The friars landed on it. There were the streets, there was
“The Silver Lion.” Nothing had changed but he, who walked through it
barefoot, with his heart calm and cold, his hands across his breast,
and his eyes bent meekly on the ground, a true son of Dominic and Holy
Church.

[Reference Rewrite]: To comprehend the architecture of my early exile, one must first understand the absolute poverty of my universe at the age of seven. I existed within a microscopic empire of two, subjugated by a man I was conditioned to call "Master." He was a square-built, brutal artifact of a world I did not know, roughly sixty years of age, though time on the island seemed measured only by the decay of his humanity. His dark hair fell in matted, feral clusters, and a vast beard obscured his face, rendering him less a man than a beast draped in the ruin of whatever civilization had cast him out. He possessed a terrifying latent power, yet he spent his days in a state of stagnant lethargy, only stirring to exert his dominance over my labor—collecting sea-birds or hauling faggots of wood down the ravine.

Our lives were bound by the daily ritual of bathing in a salt-water pool, barricaded from the shark-infested ocean by a ridge of jagged stone. Beyond this, my existence was an enforced void. I was permitted no education, no heritage, and almost no language. The Master utilized silence as a tool of oppression, rationing his words to commands and curses, ensuring my mind remained as barren as the rocky crags that caged us. I became a taciturn creature, my intellect starved, left to gaze into the abyssal depths of the ocean or trace the cold geometries of the stars. I was kept as a beast of the field—valuable only for the calories my labor saved him, and perhaps to serve as a mirror for his own desperate need for mastery.

[Reference Original]: CHAPTER THREE.

I left him, and commenced a careful descent of the precipices by which we were surrounded, but, before I had gone fifty paces, another flash of lightning was followed up by a loud shriek, which arrested my steps. Where the noise came from I could not tell, but I heard my companion calling to me to come back. I obeyed him, and found him standing where I had left him.

"You called me, master?"

"Yes, I did; take my hand and lead me to the cabin."

I obeyed him, wondering why he asked me so to do. He gained his bed-place, and threw himself down on it.

"Bring the kid full of water," said he--"quick!"

I brought it, and he bathed his head and face. After a time, he threw himself back upon the bed-place, and groaned heavily.

"O God! It's all over with me," said he at last. "I shall live and die in this cursed hole."

"What's the matter, master?" said I.

"Yes, I did. Take my hand. Lead me to the cabin."

I guided him, marveling at the sudden frailty in his grip. The hand that had so often struck me down now clung to my shoulder with the desperate dependency of a drowning man. He found his bedding and collapsed onto it, a ruined monument of flesh.

"Bring the kid full of water," he gasped. "Quick!"

I brought the vessel. He plunged his face into it, bathing his head as if trying to wash away the fire of the heavens. Presently, he fell back against the damp wood, a heavy groan escaping his chest. "O God! It is all over with me," he whispered into the gloom. "I shall live and die in this cursed hole."

"What is the matter, master?" I asked.

He offered no answer, sinking instead into a rhythmic liturgy of curses and moans. When he finally fell still, I slipped out again into the dying tempest.

Brother Clement had labored in Basel for over a year, weaving his voice through the cobblestones and confessional booths of the city, when Jerome appeared before him. Dust coated the younger friar's robes, but his eyes burned with a triumphant clarity. "Glory be to God, Brother Clement," Jerome declared, his tone vibrating with anticipation. "You may now journey to England alongside me."

"I stand ready, Brother Jerome," Clement replied, his demeanor shifting instantly from weary scholar to eager pilgrim. "I have awaited your summons for months. In the quiet intervals between teaching and prayer, I have diligently cultivated the English tongue."

"Tactful indeed," Jerome acknowledged. He explained that his delay had been necessary to secure extraordinary faculties from the Pope: the authority to collect funds for the Church's cause in England and to administer sacraments within the secular monasteries. "Now, gird your loins," Jerome commanded, his voice hardening into steel. "Let us depart and strike a decisive blow for the Church, and against the encroaching influence of the Franciscans."

Thus began their pilgrimage down the Rhine, a river that served as both artery and boundary. In the bustling metropolises, they shared the pulpit, their voices merging in a chorus of reform. Yet in the smaller hamlets, they diverged, taking opposite banks of the winding waterway until they converged once more at a preordained meeting point. Both were masters of rhetoric, yet their styles operated on distinct frequencies. Jerome's oratory was noble and imposing, a towering edifice of logic, though occasionally constrained by rigid dogma and a monotony that risked alienating the common ear. Clement, conversely, possessed a fluidity that defied categorization. His speech was a tapestry of variety, tender and gently persuasive, curling around the listener's reason and heart like smoke in a draftless room. Yet, when the moment demanded, Clement ascended. He soared with a prophetic intensity that left Jerome grounded. *Vehemens ut procella, excitatus ut torrens, incensus ut fulmen*—violent as a storm, roused as a torrent, inflamed as lightning—he thundered, flashed, and swept all before him with the rushing waves of his eloquence.

Jerome possessed the scholarly humility to admit such disparity, citing five reasons why he withheld samples of Clement's fiery Latin: the difficulty of translation, the brevity of time, prior publication, the existence of superior imitators, and the literary axiom that while uniformity suits peas, it constitutes a vice in books. Nevertheless, Clement employed a subtle strategy: he secretly investigated the specific sins plaguing each town before ascending the rostrum. Jerome, however, remained unbending, scorning the detour required to tailor his message to local vices.

At a great town situated several leagues from the Rhine, they climbed the same pulpit in succession. Jerome addressed the vanity of dress, a theme dear to his heart. He spoke with biting satire, and the congregation listened with complacent nods, for vanity was not their primary failing. Then Clement stepped forward to confront their true demon: drunkenness. It was a festering wound in these lands, shielded by clerical hypocrisy and popular prejudice. Clement delivered merciless blows drawn from Holy Writ and grim reality. He identified alcohol not merely as a vice, but as the nurturing mother of all other crimes, particularly theft and murder.

He recounted a recent parricide committed by a man intoxicated, and described how a gang of drunkards had roasted one of their own comrades alive in a neighboring village. "Your late prince," Clement proclaimed, his voice rising to a crescendo, "is rumored to have died of apoplexy, yet you know the truth: he died of drink. Last month, one of your aldermen perished miserably, drowned in his own stupor within a muddy puddle."

His gaze swept the crowd, piercing the collective shame. "Your children's backs go bare so that you may fill your bellies with the poison that turns you into the worst of beasts—silly as calves, yet fierce as boars. This deprives your families of sustenance and drives your souls straight to hell. I tell you, your town, yes, your entire nation, would sink to the bottom of human degradation if your women drank as you do. How long will they remain temperate, resisting nature to oppose the example of their husbands and fathers? Vice never stands still. Amend yourselves, or watch them descend to your level. Already in Bohemia, women drink alongside men."

"How does a drunken woman appear?" he demanded, the question hanging heavy in the air. "Would you wish to see your wives, your mothers, reduced to such a state?"

A roar of horror erupted from the assembly. Medieval audiences had not yet mastered the art of passive amusement; they reacted viscerally. "That strikes home!" cried the friar, seizing the momentum. "Do you suppose it shocks the All-Pure God less to witness a man, His noblest creation, transformed into a drunken beast, than it shocks you, creatures of sin and unreason, to see a woman degraded into something no better than yourselves?"

Clement concluded with two stark tableaux: the chaotic wreckage of a drunkard's household versus the serene order of a sober man's life. The details were so vivid, so brutally true, that the women fell into a collective swoon of "Ohing" and "Ahing," murmuring, "Eh, but that is a true word."

The discourse ignited a frenzy. Hearers clustered in knots; the men bristled with indignation. The women, however, rallied behind them, openly siding with the accused against the preacher. A married man, they argued, had a divine right to a drop; he needed it to sustain the labor of feeding his family. They refused to trade their sturdy drinkers for weak-willed "milksops." The hypocrisy was palpable.

That very evening, a mob of men cornered nearly a hundred individuals near Brother Clement, stuffing his wallet with coins and plucking roses from their own heads to offer him, kissing his habit and blessing him for undertaking the arduous task of curing their "sots."

Jerome observed the scene with a furrowed brow. "Drunkenness is not heresy, Clement," he remarked critically. "To dedicate an entire sermon to it seems... earthly."

As they continued their journey, Jerome discovered to his astonishment that Clement's serments penetrated the populace far deeper than his own. They compelled listeners to listen, to think, to weep, and occasionally, to amend their ways. "He possesses the art of sinking to their peg," Jerome mused, watching the crowds react. "Yet he retains the capacity to soar high enough at times."

On the whole, the phenomenon puzzled Jerome, who harbored a secret sense of superiority over his tenderer brother. Eventually, after traveling approximately two hundred miles, the situation ceased to puzzle him and began to displease him. He struggled to suppress the sentiment as petty and unworthy. "Souls differ like locks," Jerome reasoned aloud to himself, attempting to rationalize the divergence. "Preachers must differ like keys, or the Church remains locked shut, unable to open for God to pass through. And certainly, this novice holds the key to these northern souls, being himself a northern man."

And so they descended slowly along the Rhine, sometimes drifting a few miles downstream, but mostly walking the banks, preaching, teaching, and hearing confessions in the scattered towns and villages. Finally, they reached Düsseldorf.

There lay the small quay where Gerard and Denys had once boarded their boat upstream. The friars disembarked upon it. The streets stretched out before them, familiar and unchanged, save for the presence of "The Silver Lion." Nothing had altered in the cityscape, yet everything had shifted within the traveler who walked through it barefoot. His heart was calm and cold, his hands folded across his breast, his eyes bent meekly toward the earth—a true son of Dominic and the Holy Church, returning to a world he knew intimately, yet forever changed by the fires he had kindled.
